# Cryptography and codebreaking (ciphers, frequency analysis, one-time pad) (`cryptography`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing, probability_statistics, combinatorics_permutations, information_theory, military_intelligence_codebreaking
- Core idea: A cipher changes a message by a rule that depends on a secret key. Replacing each letter by another fixed letter looks safe, since there are more keys than anyone could try, but it is broken in minutes by counting: in any language some letters and pairs are much more frequent than others (in English, e is about one letter in eight), and the counts survive the substitution. Changing the substitution alphabet from letter to letter according to a keyword hides the counts, until the length of the keyword is found from repeated fragments and each alphabet is counted separately. The one-time pad gives perfect secrecy with a key of truly random letters as long as the message, known only to sender and receiver and never used twice (one-time pad). A sound system must stay safe even when the enemy knows everything about it except the key.
- Pitfalls:
  - Trusting a simple substitution, or any scheme, because the number of possible keys is huge
  - Relying on the method being secret; it leaks, and only the key should need protecting
  - Reusing a one-time pad or making its key by a rule or by a person 'typing at random'; Soviet reuse of pads in the 1940s let the Americans read the Venona messages
  - Stereotyped openings, repeated messages and lazy operators, which broke more ciphers, including Enigma, than mathematics alone
  - Inventing one's own cipher and judging it secure because one cannot break it oneself
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1500 BC – a cuneiform tablet hides a pottery glaze recipe behind unusual sign values; greece: 5th c. BC – the Spartan scytale (whether it was a cipher device is disputed); 4th c. BC Aeneas Tacticus on secret messages; rome: 1st c. BC – Caesar's shift of the alphabet by three places, reported by Suetonius; india: c. 3rd c. AD – the Kamasutra lists secret writing by letter substitution among the arts; islamic: 9th c. – al-Kindi's treatise on deciphering describes frequency analysis (manuscript rediscovered in Istanbul in 1987); 14th c. Ibn al-Durayhim, al-Qalqashandi; europe: c. 1467 – Alberti's cipher disc and polyalphabetic substitution; 1553 Bellaso's keyword cipher, later misnamed after Vigenère (1586); c. 1854 Babbage and 1863 Kasiski break it; 1883 Kerckhoffs's principles; 1932 Rejewski reconstructs the Enigma wiring (Warsaw); 1939–1945 Bletchley Park; americas: 1882 – Frank Miller describes a one-time key for telegrams; 1917–1919 Vernam's teleprinter cipher and Mauborgne's random non-repeating key; 1945–1949 Shannon proves the one-time pad perfect and founds the theory of secrecy systems
- Read:
  - David Kahn, The Codebreakers: The Story of Secret Writing (1967)
  - Claude E. Shannon, Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems, Bell System Technical Journal 28 (1949)
  - Simon Singh, The Code Book (1999)
